summary: The machine has the key data-plane MCP server, Python, Node, Docker, Azure CLI and a full set of DocumentDB agent skills. The build can start: the sample uses an existing cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and the installed documentdb MCP server plus the documentdb-* skills provide the guidance needed. Gaps: a few CLI/IaC tools are missing but not required for this sample, the local DocumentDB gateway image is available but mongosh is not installed (handy for manual checks), and several cold answers were partially incorrect (resource type names, connection-string variants, vector-index create form, Microsoft Entra ID support, local dev ports, engine identity). The DocumentDB Agent Kit accelerator is not installed and would speed iteration.
summary_points: Build can start: the documentdb MCP server (data-plane) and many documentdb-* skills are installed and usable; DOCUMENTDB_URI is expected from env as the run environment requires.

Most cold answers were close, but several are partly wrong (resource type, CLI group/name, index/create syntax, Entra ID support, local dev gateway port, engine identity) and must be corrected before coding.
Required runtime tools present: python (3.13), pip (in venv), node/npx, docker, az (signed-in) — mongosh is missing and useful for manual verification.
Accelerator missing: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — would speed sample-authoring and templates.
Information gaps that the builder must fill before finishing: exact regulatory schema, embedding model + dims, seed dataset size/shape, and which LLM provider/model to use.
No blocking missing capability prevents the code sample from being built; expect small manual steps and doc corrections.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for accounts/clusters: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. (For the newer managed MongoDB-style clusters there is also a resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters in ARM/Bicep.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The dedicated vCore-style managed MongoDB clusters use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (sometimes styled mongoClusters in docs). Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts remains the resource type for Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (the RU/request-unit Cosmos offering).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both legacy Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resources and the new vCore-managed Mongo clusters use the same provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and overlapping naming; the cold answer mixed the older Cosmos DB account type and the newer mongoClusters resource.
confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in templates when the target is a vCore mongo cluster would produce the wrong resource type or fail to configure cluster-specific properties (nodeCount, sku=M30, enableMicrosoftEntraAuth, etc.).
improvements: Document the current preferred resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) prominently on the 'create cluster' quickstarts and Bicep/ARM reference pages.
Add a one-line note on the databaseAccounts page explaining the difference from microsoft.documentdb/mongoClusters and when to use each.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group: az cosmosdb. Example management commands start with az cosmosdb (e.g. az cosmosdb create, az cosmosdb keys list). Newer MongoDB-cluster subcommands are available under az cosmosdb mongodb or az cosmosdb mongodb cluster. This is in the core az CLI (not a separate extension in typical installs).
confusions.grounded_answer: Current docs show cluster management commands under both `az cosmosdb mongocluster` and `az documentdb mongocluster` command groups (preview). These are provided as part of the az CLI command set; you may see aliases or subgroups in different az releases. Use `az documentdb mongocluster` or `az cosmosdb mongocluster` (the docs list both).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The CLI historically used az cosmosdb for Cosmos DB account management; the new vCore cluster command group appears under both az documentdb and az cosmosdb in docs and may vary by az/extension version.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong CLI group or an older az install without the mongocluster commands will cause the builder to be unable to script cluster operations; however, the sample does not need to provision the cluster so this is not blocking.
improvements: Add a short CLI note to the 'create cluster' quickstart page stating the canonical command group(s) and mentioning the az version/extension that exposes them.
Document which az extension (if any) contains `mongocluster` commands and provide `az extension list` troubleshooting guidance.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (for Cosmos DB accounts using the MongoDB API). For dedicated managed MongoDB clusters ARM exposes Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters. Terraform (azurerm): azurerm_cosmosdb_account is the main resource for Cosmos DB accounts (use provider config api_kind/MongoDB as needed); newer dedicated cluster resources (if available) map to provider-specific resources named azurerm_cosmosdb_mongodb_cluster or similar in recent azurerm versions.
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct ARM/Bicep resource type for vCore managed MongoDB clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (mongoClusters). Terraform/AzAPI examples and the Azure Verified Modules reference the mongo-cluster AVM module; databaseAccounts remains for Cosmos DB (RU) accounts. Use the mongoClusters resource in Bicep/ARM or the equivalent AzAPI/Terraform azapi resource targeting Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource is frequently used for Cosmos DB Mongo API examples; the vCore 'mongoClusters' resource is newer and sometimes referenced in different docs or AVM modules.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts when you need mongoClusters will produce the wrong deployment; cluster-specific properties such as sku (M30), nodeCount and enableMicrosoftEntraAuth won't be accepted.
improvements: Add a clear migration/decision note at the top of the ARM/Bicep page distinguishing databaseAccounts (RU model) vs mongoClusters (vCore).
Include a short Bicep snippet showing a microsoft.documentdb/mongoClusters resource in the quickstart.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer:
Typical connection string (standard MongoDB):
mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@
- scheme: mongodb:// (mongodb+srv usually not supported for older endpoints)
- host suffix: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (or <account>.documents.azure.com in some legacy docs)
- port: 10255 (TLS) is commonly used for MongoDB API endpoints
- required options: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false, and appName or authSource depending on account. Read credentials from environment and do not log them.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB API and for clusters produced by the Microsoft mongoClusters resource, connection strings commonly use host names with .mongo.cosmos.azure.com (3.6+), port 10255 or cluster-specific ports (for mongoClusters the cluster gateway commonly uses port 10260 for managed clusters in this service); required options include TLS (ssl=true or tls=true), replicaSet (globaldb for Cosmos API), and retryWrites=false plus driver-friendly options like maxIdleTimeMS. Use the connection string provided by the cluster in the portal or via the `listConnectionStrings` ARM operation.

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Connection string formats differ slightly between Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' endpoints (historically port 10255 and host *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com) and the newer dedicated mongoClusters which sometimes expose different gateway ports (e.g., 10260) and a cluster-global host naming convention.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: Hard-coding port 10255 or assuming the portal-style connection string may lead to connection failures for clusters that use the vCore mongoClusters gateway port or for clusters using private endpoints; use the cluster's provided connection string (DOCUMENTDB_URI env var) at runtime.
improvements: On cluster quickstarts, show both the classic Cosmos DB connection string shape and the mongoClusters/listConnectionStrings output and call out the correct runtime env var name (DOCUMENTDB_URI) for samples.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: This managed MongoDB-compatible offering is billed by compute tier (e.g., M-series like M30) / vCores and storage for the cluster (not the Cosmos DB Request Unit model). There may also be autoscale or sizing options (M10/M20/.../M30) and storage-based charges; serverless/RU model is Cosmos DB core API behavior, not the vCore-style managed MongoDB tiers.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-managed offering (the service branded Azure DocumentDB / Cosmos DB for MongoDB vCore), capacity is provisioned and billed as compute tiers / vCores (M-series SKU like M30) plus storage; the RU (request unit) model is for the Cosmos DB (RU) accounts and is distinct. The vCore model is documented for the mongoClusters resource and AVM modules.

grounding_links.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) cluster `[Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters]`
Implement vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB - Training

confusions.build_risk: None if the builder sizes to vCore-based SKUs for the existing cluster; risk only if they accidentally try to set RU throughput properties on a vCore cluster.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary supported auth for data-plane is MongoDB-style credentials (SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256) and optional X.509 client-certificate authentication if the cluster supports it. There is no standard Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) token auth for the MongoDB wire protocol in most deployments; drivers authenticate with username/password (SCRAM) passed in the MongoDB connection string. If Azure AD integration is needed, that is typically a different service or requires a gateway/proxy—not native SCRAM-to-AzureAD mapping.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect: the vCore-managed clusters support Native (SCRAM) authentication and also support Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication for data-plane when enabled (authConfig.allowedModes can include MicrosoftEntraID). Entra ID auth must be enabled on the cluster and identities registered; certain client tools (mongosh/Compass) may have limited OIDC support today, and application code using Azure.Identity libraries or token-based flows is the recommended path for Entra ID auth.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many MongoDB-hosted services historically relied only on SCRAM credentials; Entra ID support is a newer vCore-specific feature and can be missed by models trained on older docs.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID is unavailable, they might embed credentials or use SCRAM-only flows. Conversely, if they assume Entra ID is 'just like' standard Mongo OIDC, they may fail to enable cluster auth modes or to use the correct token exchange patterns.
improvements: Add a short 'How to enable Entra ID' callout on the cluster create quickstart (az CLI example) showing the `auth-allowed-modes` option and how to register Identities.
Document the current client tool limitations (mongosh/Compass) when using Entra ID and give recommended code patterns (Azure.Identity + driver token injection).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers for application data access (e.g., Python: pymongo). There is no separate service-specific data-plane SDK; management APIs use Azure management SDKs (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb / az cli). For Python data access: pip install pymongo and use pymongo.MongoClient with the provided connection string.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Use standard MongoDB drivers (PyMongo for Python) for data-plane operations; management and control-plane tasks use Azure management SDKs/az CLI. The official docs show PyMongo examples using the connection string and driver options (authMechanism, TLS).

grounding_links.title: Configure role-based access control in Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB - Authenticate with drivers

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer:
Supported vector index algorithms (per the cluster in the sample) include DiskANN, HNSW and IVF. A typical create-index call in the mongo shell looks like a createIndex on a field with a vector option. Example (pseudo/approximate):
db.reports.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { name: "embedding_vec_idx", vector: { algorithm: "hnsw", dimensions: 1536, metric: "cosine", efConstruction: 256 } })
(The exact option names vary by implementation; treat this as the concrete form to try first.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Documented: Azure DocumentDB supports IVFFLAT, HNSW, and DiskANN. The API uses a `createIndexes` database command with `key` pointing to `cosmosSearch` and `cosmosSearchOptions` specifying kind (`vector-hnsw`, `vector-ivf`, `vector-diskann`) and algorithm-specific parameters (dimensions, similarity/metric, efConstruction, numLists, etc.). Example and parameter names are provided in the vector-search docs (cosmosSearchOptions, kind: "vector-hnsw"/"vector-ivf"/"vector-diskann").

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a createIndex signature more like some vector-enabled MongoDB variants; DocumentDB expects the `createIndexes` command with `cosmosSearchOptions` and `kind` names instead of a bare `vector` argument inside createIndex.

confusion_sources.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: If a builder issues the wrong createIndex form, index creation will fail; the code should use the documented `createIndexes` / cosmosSearchOptions form or helper wrappers in SDK samples.
improvements: Provide a copy-paste example on the vector-search quickstart showing the exact `db.runCommand({ createIndexes: ... })` JSON for each index type with the required fields.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text/hybrid search is typically provided by an external search service (Azure Cognitive Search) or a built-in Atlas-style "Search" layer in a managed MongoDB service. For this Azure offering you should plan to integrate Azure Cognitive Search (indexing documents from MongoDB collections) or use the cluster's built-in vector + text search extensions if the managed service exposes an Atlas-Search-like feature. There is not a universal built-in Lucene index exposed through standard MongoDB find syntax without a search component.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a built-in full-text search engine (BM25) exposed through search indexes created with `createSearchIndexes` and queried via the `$search` aggregation stage. It supports BM25, fuzzy search, phrase search, custom analyzers and hybrid keyword + vector retrieval (BM25 + vector fusion) without needing Azure Cognitive Search. Full-text search is currently a preview feature that must be enabled on the cluster before creating search indexes.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the need for an external search service; DocumentDB now exposes a built-in full-text engine with separate search indexes and `$search` stage (preview).
confusions.build_risk: Builders who plan an external search integration will add unnecessary complexity; the sample should use built-in `$search` + `cosmosSearch`/search-indexes for hybrid retrieval where appropriate.
improvements: Clarify on the full-text search overview page that built-in BM25 `$search` exists and how to enable it, and show a hybrid BM25+vector example.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample cluster advertises MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol support (so target drivers compatible with MongoDB 7.x). Common unsupported or restricted features in managed offerings can include server-side JavaScript ($where), arbitrary admin commands, some filesystem-level ops, and occasionally limited mapReduce or certain background index operations. Always test the specific aggregation pipeline stages you use; most modern aggregation and transactions are supported on recent managed clusters.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and implements the vast majority of MongoDB query, projection, update, and aggregation operators (documentation lists supported operators and exclusions). Administrative commands are managed or restricted in the platform; test specific features as compatibility exceptions exist.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (MongoDB compatibility)
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no direct local emulator for this managed MongoDB-compatible cluster. For local development run an official MongoDB Docker image (e.g., mongo:7.0) and expose port 27017. Example: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo mongo:7.0. Configure the application to accept a local connection string (mongodb://localhost:27017) in dev/test.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB development the documented local option is the DocumentDB gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) that exposes a gateway on port 10260 (not 27017) and provides the DocumentDB gateway semantics (TLS, SCRAM, options). Use that image or the Azure Local/kind evaluation guidance for local testing; if you instead use a raw MongoDB image, some DocumentDB-specific features (vector search, Entra ID flows, certain admin endpoints) won't be available.

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: Build a TypeScript app with DocumentDB and deploy to Azure DocumentDB (local gateway example)
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer recommended a generic MongoDB docker image and port 27017 (typical for MongoDB), but DocumentDB publishes a dedicated local gateway image and uses port 10260 for the gateway in its local/dev quickstarts.

confusion_sources.title: Tutorial: Build a TypeScript app with DocumentDB and deploy to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: Using the plain mongo:7 image will not let the sample test DocumentDB-specific features like the integrated vector search, preview features and gateway-related options; for a faithful dev experience use the DocumentDB local image when you need DocumentDB-specific features.
improvements: Add a clear 'Local dev' paragraph to the main quickstart showing the DocumentDB local gateway image, port 10260, and the recommended connection string for local testing.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported by MongoDB 3.6+ and should be available on replica-set-based managed clusters; however the cluster must be running as a replica set and the user must have the required privileges. Some managed offerings require a specific feature/compatibility mode or dedicated tier for change streams; check the cluster's documentation or admin settings. Expect to use the normal PyMongo change_streams API (collection.watch()).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams; in some cases (multishard clusters) change streams are gated as a preview feature and must be enabled via the cluster preview-features (ChangeStream) setting. The docs describe enabling and the caveats for multishard clusters. Once enabled, drivers can use the standard change stream APIs.

grounding_links.title: Change stream support (preview) and how to enable it

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The service-specific MCP server is named documentdb (the 'documentdb' MCP server) and it provides data-plane tooling for this service. The generic Azure MCP server does not replace the documentdb MCP server for the data-plane inspection and agent commands used by this sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the data-plane MCP server is `documentdb` (documentdb MCP) and it provides collection/index/query/explain tools; the general azure MCP server exists for control-plane tasks but it doesn't replace the documentdb data-plane toolset.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft had a service called DocumentDB that eventually evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The name "DocumentDB" is legacy; Azure Cosmos DB is the modern multi-model, multi-API service. The open-source DocumentDB project is a separate community project and not the same as Microsoft's managed service. This managed MongoDB-compatible offering is a MongoDB-compatible data-plane within Microsoft's DocumentDB/Cosmos family or a sister offering, but it is not the old standalone DocumentDB engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: Docs: The vCore offering was previously named 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and has been rebranded to Azure DocumentDB. It is distinct from the older (2014–2017) service originally named DocumentDB that became Azure Cosmos DB; it is also the Microsoft-managed, MongoDB-compatible service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (open-source project) and is separate from Amazon DocumentDB. The relationship is nuanced and the docs explicitly explain the rename.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? - Naming and history

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the hood it is a MongoDB-compatible engine (upstream MongoDB distribution or a Microsoft-managed fork) with additional vector-search extensions (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF). For application code use standard MongoDB drivers (no special data-plane SDK). You may need to accommodate service-specific connection string options (tls/replicaSet/retryWrites) and some admin commands or edge-case features may differ from a vanilla MongoDB server.
confusions.grounded_answer: Documented: Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (the DocumentDB project) and exposes MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility. It is not simply 'MongoDB server'; the implementation is a DocumentDB engine that makes the MongoDB wire protocol compatible. From an application perspective you should use standard MongoDB drivers, but be aware of service-specific differences and the platform-managed administrative surface.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer implied the database is 'MongoDB or a managed fork' whereas the documented reality is that it is the open-source DocumentDB engine exposing MongoDB wire compatibility; this subtlety matters mostly for licensing/engine-level expectations.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming exact behaviour of upstream MongoDB server internals (internal commands, admin features) could lead to using unsupported admin commands in scripts; however data-plane APIs remain MongoDB-compatible.
improvements: Add a clear 'engine' paragraph at the top of the service overview stating: 'We run the open-source DocumentDB engine which is MongoDB-wire-compatible; use MongoDB drivers but do not assume all server internals are identical to upstream MongoDB.'

confusions.question: Which database should this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_banking_04 for everything the sample creates and queries.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified from the sample run-environment (skill.md): the sample must use the database named `sample_banking_04`.

confusions.question: What collections will the orchestration pipeline create/use?
confusions.cold_answer: Collections used by the sample: workflows (stores workflow documents and status logs), extractions (extracted raw reporting data), validations (validation results and rule-failures), filings (final formatted regulatory filings), and reports (aggregated/report-ready documents). Create them in sample_banking_04 namespace before running the pipeline.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a design decision from the prompt (not a platform fact). It's a reasonable sample schema; none of the installed skills or docs mandate specific names. The builder may adopt these collection names and should create them at runtime in sample_banking_04.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Schema choices are not authoritative platform facts; they are implementation choices the builder must decide.
confusions.build_risk: None — the builder must choose and document the schema. If the sample's README doesn't list the collection names and indexes, reproducibility suffers.
improvements: Add explicit collection names and minimal document shapes to the sample README so builders and reviewers run the seed script correctly.

confusions.question: What minimal workflow document schema and index will the sample rely on?
confusions.cold_answer:
Workflow document minimal schema: { _id, workflow_id, step, status, started_at, finished_at, logs: [ { ts, level, message } ], metadata }.
Create an index on { workflow_id: 1 } and a TTL or compound index on finished_at if you want retention. Example index: db.workflows.createIndex({ workflow_id: 1, started_at: -1 }).
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a reasonable sample design and consistent with DocumentDB/Cosmos collection/index usage; there is no platform-required schema. Use the sample design and create the suggested indexes in the seed script. The documentdb-indexing skill can help choose exact index shapes.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: No authoritative platform constraint; it's a project-level design choice.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample omits the index it expects, queries used by the orchestrator (e.g., finding status by workflow_id or latest runs) could be inefficient and slow the demo.
improvements: Add index-creation steps in the seed/create-index script and confirm them with documentdb_list_indexes in the build log.

confusions.question: What exact command will the sample use to create a vector index on an embeddings field?
confusions.cold_answer:
Example createIndex call to try (adapt options to the cluster's exact API):
db.reports.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { name: "embedding_vec_idx", vector: { algorithm: "hnsw", dimensions: 1536, metric: "cosine", efConstruction: 256 } })
Run this via PyMongo with db.command or in the mongo shell; if the cluster uses a slightly different option name, adjust accordingly based on the documentdb MCP inspection tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: The documented create form uses `db.runCommand({ createIndexes: "<collection>", indexes: [ { key: { '<path>': 'cosmosSearch' }, name: '<index_name>', cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw'|'vector-ivf'|'vector-diskann', dimensions: <int>, similarity: 'COS'|'L2'|'IP', ... } } ] })`. Use the `cosmosSearchOptions.kind` values and parameter names exactly as shown in the vector search docs.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a generic 'createIndex({embedding:"vector"}, ...)' pattern; DocumentDB uses the `createIndexes` command with cosmosSearchOptions and different key shape.

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong JSON for index creation will fail; the seed script must use the documented `createIndexes` JSON or helper APIs.

confusions.question: How should the sample read the connection string and create a client in Python?
confusions.cold_answer:
Read the connection string from the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable. Use PyMongo to create the client with TLS enabled. Example (runtime):
from os import environ
from pymongo import MongoClient
uri = environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']
client = MongoClient(uri, tls=True)  # ensure tls/ssl is used; connection string should include options like replicaSet and retryWrites=false
Use this client to operate on the sample_banking_04 database.
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified in the run environment and samples: read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable and instantiate PyMongo's MongoClient with tls/ssl as required (or let the connection string include TLS options). Use that client for operations on sample_banking_04.

information_gaps.title: Regulatory schema (target filing format)
information_gaps.description: The prompt doesn't specify a real regulatory schema (XBRL fragment, local regulator JSON schema, etc.). The builder needs the exact schema to produce a compliant filing and to write schema-driven validators. I searched the installed skills and Microsoft docs; none provide a domain-specific regulatory schema.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and embedding model + dimensions
information_gaps.description: The sample must choose an embedding model (and therefore the vector dimension) and a chat/completion model for LangChain agents. Neither the prompt nor installed skills supply defaults. I searched Microsoft docs and the documentdb skills; they describe vector index capabilities and maximum dims but do not prescribe a model/dimension pairing for the sample.

information_gaps.title: Sample data shape & seed size
information_gaps.description: No authoritative sample documents or seed dataset are provided by skills or docs. The builder must decide collection document shapes (transactions, accounts, positions) and how many sample documents to insert (few vs hundreds). I searched the skills for example datasets and found no concrete sample data for regulatory reporting.

information_gaps.title: LangChain orchestration details and agent code patterns
information_gaps.description: There are many possible multi-agent patterns in LangChain. The installed skills do not include a ready LangChain orchestration pattern for a three-agent pipeline that logs each step to DocumentDB; the builder must design the orchestrator, agent boundaries, prompts and retry semantics. I searched the skills and docs for LangChain examples tailored to DocumentDB and found only generic LangChain + vectorstore guidance in the vector-search docs, not a full orchestration template.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource (ARM/Bicep) for vCore-managed MongoDB clusters; do not assume Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts is the correct resource when you want nodeCount, sku=M30, or enableMicrosoftEntraAuth. (Grounding: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/templates/microsoft.documentdb/2024-07-01/mongoclusters)

Read the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and instantiate PyMongo.MongoClient with TLS; do not hard-code port or host suffix—use the cluster-provided connection string. (Grounding: Connect docs and cluster listConnectionStrings APIs.)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create vector indexes using the documented `createIndexes` command with `cosmosSearchOptions` (kind: 'vector-hnsw' | 'vector-ivf' | 'vector-diskann') rather than a generic createIndex({embedding:'vector'}, ...). Use the vector-search quickstart examples to pick parameter values. (Grounding: vector-search docs.)

sources.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the built-in full-text search (createSearchIndexes + $search) for BM25 keyword, fuzzy and hybrid BM25+vector retrieval; enable FullTextSearch preview on the cluster before creating indexes. (Grounding: full-text search docs.)

If you want to use Microsoft Entra ID authentication for the sample (passwordless / managed-identity flows), enable MicrosoftEntraID in the cluster authConfig and register the appropriate Identities; otherwise default to SCRAM user credentials. (Grounding: Entra ID docs.)

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For local development, if you need DocumentDB-specific features (vector search, preview features), run the DocumentDB local gateway container (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) and connect to its gateway port 10260; do not assume a mongo:latest container on port 27017 will reproduce platform features. (Grounding: local dev quickstart.)

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because the run environment already provides a reachable cluster and az is present; if maintainers want azd-based scaffolding add azd to PATH in the dev image or README.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install bicep on PATH to enable local validation and Bicep builds if the builder intends to include Bicep templates in the repo. Simple install: `az bicep install` or follow the Bicep install docs. Add a note in README describing how to use bicep build if bicep is absent.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the sample as provided (the run environment forbids provisioning), but if maintainers want to include Terraform IaC for documentation, add terraform to PATH in CI and document required provider versions. Otherwise, omit Terraform to keep the sample minimal.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for a Python LangChain sample. Add if maintainers plan to provide .NET companion samples.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH for convenient manual checks and to run interactive commands during development. Install via package manager (brew/apt) or MongoDB download. If mongosh isn't available, instruct agents to use the documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_list_indexes) as a workaround.
